definitions.definition: Śakti — the totality of powers, the 'family' of the Goddess, her yoginīs and mothers, and the manifest world; paired with akula, Śiva (Kulārṇava 17.27).
The Goddess's family of powers ordered in the six centres; the Kubjikāmata calls itself the Kula lineage of the Kulālikāmnāya.
Śiva, beyond the totality of powers (Kulārṇava 17.27).
The Kula path and its initiate; the highest of the seven modes of conduct (Kulārṇava 2.7-8), of the nature of both enjoyment and yoga (2.23).
The initiate of the Kula, skilled in joining Kula and Akula (Kulārṇava 17.27); knower of the seven ullāsas (8.95).
The Goddess as head of the Kula, addressed throughout the Kulārṇava; worshipped with Kuleśvara/Bhairava.
The Kaula way itself, in which enjoyment becomes yoga, sin merit, and saṃsāra liberation (Kulārṇava 2.24); those established in it do not return to rebirth (2.30).
The rules of conduct of the Kaula, taught in Kulārṇava 11 — honouring women and Kula yogins, keeping the samayas, secrecy.
The seven modes: Veda, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Siddhānta and Kaula, each higher than the last (Kulārṇava 2.7-8).
The first mode: Vedic ritual conduct.
The second mode: devotion to Viṣṇu with vegetarian purity.
The third mode: Śaiva worship.
The fourth mode: 'right-hand' worship of the Goddess without the Kaula substances (or with substitutes); in Bengal the usual mode of Kālī worship.
The fifth mode: 'left-hand' worship with the Kaula substances, reserved for the vīra (summary only).
The sixth mode, above the Vāma (Kulārṇava 2.8).
The seventh and highest mode, beyond which there is nothing (Kulārṇava 2.8)
The mode of worship of Tārā/Nīlasarasvatī learned in Mahācīna; Vasiṣṭha was sent there by the Goddess and taught the Kula way by the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).
The 'Buddhist land' beyond the Himalaya to which Vasiṣṭha was sent to learn the Goddess's Kula worship (Rudrayāmala 17.122-125).
A Kaula transmission: five from Śiva's five faces — Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern and Upper (Kulārṇava 3.7); the Upper is supreme (3.15-19).
The Paścimāmnāya is the Kubjikā transmission, 'the western of all paths' (Kubjikāmata 2.21).
The Eastern transmission; in the Kashmir–Nepal scheme usually the Kula/Trika worship of Kuleśvarī and Kuleśvara (moderate confidence).
The Southern transmission; in the later scheme the cult of Kāmeśvarī / Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā).
The Western transmission: the cult of Kubjikā and Navātman (Kubjikāmata 2.21-22).
The Northern transmission: the cults of Kālī (Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, Guhyakālī) and the Krama.
The Upper transmission, declared highest and the direct means to liberation (Kulārṇava 3.15-19).

The consecrated substances of Kaula worship (the five tattvas); held to manifest the bliss of Brahman in the body when used within the rite, and condemned outside it (Kulārṇava 5.72-80; 5.96-105). Summary only.
Wine, meat, fish, mudrā (parched grain) and maithuna, the five 'realities' of Śakti worship (Mahānirvāṇa 1.57; 5.22). Restricted: summary only.
In the Kālīvilāsa's view not to be used in the Kali age, when only the paśu disposition is allowed (Kālīvilāsa 4.2-3).

equivalents.note: two names for the same five

definitions.definition: The five tattvas named by their initial 'm': madya, māṃsa, matsya, mudrā, maithuna. Restricted: summary only.
Among the five tattvas, mudrā denotes parched grain eaten in the rite, not the hand-gesture (Mahānirvāṇa 5.22).

literal: seal; gesture; (in the five M's) parched grain

definitions.definition: The substitute prescribed in place of a Kaula substance for those not eligible or in the Kali age — e.g. the 'sweet triad' of milk, sugar and honey for wine (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171), one's own wife only for the last tattva (6.14).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa pumpkin, sugarcane and spirits are 'equal to' an animal victim, and coconut water or honey replace wine for the twice-born (67.23; 67.114-115).
A substitute offering (e.g. a gourd or sugarcane in place of an animal) as allowed in the Kālikā Purāṇa and later practice.
Milk, sugar and honey, offered as if wine by householders in the Kali age (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171).
A Kaula term for menstrual blood as a sacred substance in certain rites. Restricted: named only.

notes: Named in several late Kaula tantras (e.g. Yoni and Mātṛkābheda Tantras) as reported in secondary literature; not checked.

definitions.definition: The practitioner's disposition that governs the mode of worship: paśu, vīra or divya; the Kālīvilāsa assigns them to the ages and allows only paśu in the Kali age (4.2-3; 6.10-16).

The first disposition — ritually pure worship without the Kaula substances; 'always pure' (Kālīvilāsa 6.10), the only one allowed in the Kali age by the Kālīvilāsa, and the beginning of the path in the Buddha's teaching to Vasiṣṭha (Rudrayāmala 17.137).
The second disposition, of the fearless adept who worships with the Kaula substances and in the cremation ground (summary only); by the Kālīvilāsa's account proper to the Tretā–Dvāpara ages.
The highest disposition, in which the worshipper sees all as divine; by the Kālīvilāsa's account proper to the Satya–Tretā ages.
In Kaula usage the uninitiated or the one in the paśu disposition, from whom Kula knowledge is kept; the guru 'takes up the paśu' as disciple (Kulārṇava 13.79).
The Kaula adept of the heroic disposition; fearless, beyond shame and doubt (Kulārṇava 5.82).

The seven degrees of inner exhilaration in the Kula rite — ārambha, taruṇa, yauvana, prauḍha, tadanta, unmanā, anavastha (Kulārṇava 8.4); the first five are 'waking', unmanā is 'dream', the equal state is 'deep sleep' (8.94-95). The Kulārṇava's chapters are also called ullāsas.
The sixth ullāsa, called 'dream' (Kulārṇava 8.94).

equivalents.note: the haṭha unmanī is the mind-free state of samādhi; the Kaula unmanā is a named stage of ullāsa

definitions.definition: The circle of Kaula worship in which all castes are twice-born and all are equal to Śiva, but separate again when it ends (Kulārṇava 8.96-97; Mahānirvāṇa 8.151-154). Restricted: summary only.
The circle in which the participants realise 'all is Brahman' (Mahānirvāṇa 8.208).
The state said to arise in the Kula rite, with the vision of sameness everywhere (Kulārṇava 5.74).
The pledges and rules binding the initiate; without the samaya discipline there is no perfection (Kulārṇava 5.96).
The pledges which tāmasa disciples fail to honour, becoming 'dead while living' (Kubjikāmata 12.4-9).
The guru's sandals and the mantra of the lineage's feet; 'there is no mantra beyond the pādukā' (Kulārṇava 12.12).
'Gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover (Kulārṇava 17.7); the guru is father, mother and Maheśvara (12.49); rare is the guru who removes the disciple's suffering (13.108).
Initiation by touch, sight or piercing (sparśa, dṛk, vedha), given only after mutual testing (Kulārṇava 14); there is no initiation higher than the Śākta (12.12).
The rarest initiation, in which the guru's power pierces the disciple's centres; rare is the guru who can give it (Kulārṇava 13.79; 14.66).
The guru, meditating on Śiva, touches the disciple's body (Kulārṇava 14.53).
The guru, absorbed in the highest reality, looks fully at the disciple (Kulārṇava 14.55).
The full Kaula consecration; those consecrated by it are Śaiva avadhūtas (Mahānirvāṇa 14.144).
In the Mahānirvāṇa, the saṃnyāsa of the Kali age (8.221); four kinds, complete (paramahaṃsa) and incomplete (14.142-149).
The vīra renunciant who holds 'I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava' (Nirvāṇa Tantra 14.6).

The goddesses of the Kula — sky-going, mother and earth-going — through whom Kaula knowledge descended; in Kāmarūpa the Kaula scripture is 'in every yoginī's house' (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.11-15; 22.10).
Goddesses of the six centres of the Kubjikā system (Kubjikāmata 15).

literal: female yogin; goddess of the Kula

definitions.definition: The circle of sixty-four yoginīs worshipped in hypaethral circular temples (Hirapur, Ranipur-Jharial, Bheraghat, Mitaoli); their names differ between lists.
Trees in which the Kula yoginīs always dwell; one should not eat from their leaves but worship them (Kulārṇava 11.66).
Kula: the Goddess as the totality of powers, whose union with Śiva is bliss and liberation (Kulārṇava 5.79; 17.27).
The power without which Śiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25); Kālī as the Ādyā Śakti who devours time.
Kālī as the primordial Śakti and giver of nirvāṇa (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.41; Mahānirvāṇa 4.32).
The deluding aspect of the root Nature, by which creation proceeds (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.102); in Bengal and Assam a common name of the Goddess.
Śiva, partless, all-knowing, without qualities, being–consciousness–bliss (Kulārṇava 1.7-8).
A part of Śiva like a spark of fire, covered by ignorance (Kulārṇava 1.8-9); bound it is jīva, freed it is Sadāśiva (9.42-43).
The beginningless ignorance covering the jīvas (Kulārṇava 1.9).
The subtle body that persists from birth to birth until liberation (Kulārṇava 1.11).
The form of Brahman residing in the body; the bliss of the union of Śakti and Śiva is liberation (Kulārṇava 5.79-80).
Enjoyment, which in the Kula dharma 'becomes yoga' (Kulārṇava 2.24).
The double fruit of Kaula practice (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.15; Kulārṇava 3.11).

She who devours (kalana) Time: because she devours Mahākāla she is the primordial Kālikā (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32); black because all beings enter her as colours enter black (13.5-6); standing on Śiva as a corpse (Toḍala 1.20-25).
The Mother of the Śyāmā-saṅgīt; Dakṣiṇakālī of the Tantrasāra.

literal: the Black One; she of Time

definitions.definition: The act of devouring (grasana) that gives Mahākāla and Kālī their names (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32 with Hariharānanda's gloss).
Śiva who devours all beings; Kālī devours him (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31); Dakṣiṇakālī's Bhairava (Toḍala 1.3).
Kālī as primordial Śakti, whose abode is in the thousand-petalled lotus and from whom Brahmā and the gods arise and into whom they dissolve (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.38-43).
The four-armed Kālī on Śiva as a corpse, with sword and severed head, fear-dispelling and boon-giving hands (Kālī Tantra as quoted in the Tantrasāra); consort Mahākāla (Toḍala 1.3).

literal: Kālī 'of the south' / the propitious Kālī

definitions.definition: Bengal's name for Dakṣiṇakālī (the Tantrasāra's Śyāmā section); the 'Śyāmā' of the devotional songs.

equivalents.note: in Bengal Śyāmā usually denotes Dakṣiṇakālī

definitions.definition: The cremation-ground form of Kālī worshipped by vīra practitioners and in Bengal's burning grounds.
A form of Kālī widely worshipped (in Kerala and elsewhere) as the fierce protectress; in the Kālīkula one of Kālī's forms.
The many-faced Kālī of the Nepalese Uttarāmnāya, treated in the Mahākāla Saṃhitā.
Śiva without Śakti: 'with Śakti he is Śiva, without Śakti a corpse' (Toḍala 1.25); hence Kālī stands on him.
Kālī's dwelling (Kālī Tantra dhyāna in the Tantrasāra) and the place of the vīra's night worship (Karpūrādistotra). Restricted practices summary only.
The garland of severed heads worn by Kālī (Kālī Tantra dhyāna); later Bengali interpretation reads its fifty heads as the fifty letters (moderate confidence).
The ten goddesses — Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā — as forms of the one Goddess (Muṇḍamālā in the Tantrasāra; Toḍala 1 and 10).
Satī's ten forms shown to Śiva before Dakṣa's sacrifice (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.125-134).
A mantra that needs no preliminary tests; said of the Mahāvidyās by the Muṇḍamālā, a statement Kṛṣṇānanda reads as praise (Tantrasāra).
A feminine mantra and the goddess it embodies; the ten 'great vidyās'.

The second Mahāvidyā; Akṣobhya is her Bhairava because he drank the poison without agitation (Toḍala 1.4-6); the Toḍala makes her the Fish avatāra; linked with Mahācīna and the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).

cross_language.note: the Buddhist saviour goddess Tārā; the Hindu tantras themselves place Tārā worship in Mahācīna with the Buddha

definitions.definition: The fierce form of Tārā whose five-syllable mantra perfected Buddha and Vasiṣṭha (Tārā Tantra 1.3-4).
Tārā as goddess of speech, the deity of the Bṛhannīla Tantra.
A form or companion of Tārā in the Tārā cycle.
The third Mahāvidyā, Tripurasundarī of the sixteen-syllable mantra; the Bṛhaddharma lists Ṣoḍaśī and Sundarī separately.
As a Mahāvidyā, worshipped with the five-faced Śiva as her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.7-9) and matched with Paraśurāma (10.10); her full cult is Śrīvidyā (U23).

literal: the beautiful one of the three cities

definitions.definition: The fourth Mahāvidyā; Tryambaka is her Bhairava, who delights in her in heaven, earth and the underworld (Toḍala 1.9-10); matched with Vāmana (10.10).
The fifth Mahāvidyā (Tripurabhairavī); Dakṣiṇāmūrti is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.11); matched with Balabhadra (10.10); in the Bṛhaddharma Satī herself is Bhairavī.
The sixth Mahāvidyā; her Bhairava is Kabandha, by whose worship one becomes lord of all powers (Toḍala 1.12-13); matched with Nṛsiṃha (10.9).
The seventh Mahāvidyā, 'bearing the form of a widow' and so without a Bhairava (Toḍala 1.13); matched with Varāha (10.9).
The eighth Mahāvidyā; the one-faced Mahārudra, destroyer of the world, is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.14); matched with Kūrma (10.9); goddess of paralysing (stambhana).
The ninth Mahāvidyā; Mataṅga (Dakṣiṇāmūrti) is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.15); matched with Rāma (10.10); also worshipped as Ucchiṣṭa-Mātaṅgī.
The tenth Mahāvidyā (Kamalātmikā), a tantric Lakṣmī; Sadāśiva in Viṣṇu's form is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.16).
The goddess of the Paścimāmnāya, who emerged from the liṅga and became bent out of shame (Kubjikāmata 2.3-5; 2.14); praised as the coiled power (2.2).

equivalents.note: the hymn of KMT 2.2 describes her as 'coiled like a sleeping serpent'; she is also a cult goddess with her own consort and maṇḍala

definitions.definition: Kubjikā's consort Bhairava (also Kujeśa, Śrīnātha), addressed as 'Kujeśvara' in the Kubjikāmata.
The shame by which the Goddess became bent (kubjikā) when asked for the transmission (Kubjikāmata 2.14).
Where the Kubjikā teaching was first given (Kubjikāmata 1, 'Candradvīpāvatāra'; 2.21).
Where the Kaula scripture came down, brought by Matsyendra (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 22.12).
The seat named because the Goddess 'flew up' (oḍḍitā) there (Kubjikāmata 2.40); the 'body' (piṇḍa) level of the fourfold yoni (11.7).
Uḍḍīyāna, where Satī's thighs fell (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.41).
The 'word' (pada) level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where Satī's breasts fell; the goddess there is Caṇḍī (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.43, 18.49).
The 'form' (rūpa) level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where Satī's shoulders and neck fell; the goddess there is Pūrṇeśvarī (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.43, 18.49).
Assam; the seat where Satī's yoni fell at Kāmagiri and Kāmākhyā dwells (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42, 18.49).
Kāmākhya is the 'beyond form' level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where the Kaula scripture is found in every yoginī's house (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 22.10).
A sacred seat of the Goddess where a part of Satī's body fell and Śiva stays as a liṅga (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.46).
The four seats as levels of the supreme yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7).
A lesser seat added to the lists of the major pīṭhas (Pīṭhanirṇaya and Bengali lists).
The Goddess's yoni fallen at Kāmagiri, worshipped at Kāmākhyā; Kāmākhyā is 'the great vidyā in the form of the yoni' (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42; Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4).
The supreme primal yoni of the supreme, fourfold (Kubjikāmata 11.6).
The Goddess of Kāmarūpa, worshipped at the yoni-pīṭha on Nīlācala; she is dharma, artha, kāma and liberation (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.9).

The three days in the month of Āṣāḍha (June) when the Earth — and at Kāmākhyā the Goddess — is held to menstruate; the Kāmākhyā temple is closed and reopens on the fourth day (the Ambubachi Melā). The Prāṇatoṣiṇī lists 'ambuvācī, three days' in its festival calendar.
The offering of a victim to the Goddess, taught in the Kālikā Purāṇa's offering chapter with its substitutes and restrictions (67). Restricted: summary only.

The six rites of worldly power — pacifying, subjugating, paralysing, dissension, driving away and killing — which the Mahāvidyās are said to accomplish for worshippers (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.132-133). Recorded as a teaching only.
The Goddess addressed as Mother in Bengali devotion; the songs of Rāmprasād and Kamalākānta speak to her as her child.
The Bengali devotional song genre addressed to Kālī, founded by Rāmprasād and continued by Kamalākānta.
Bengali songs of Umā's homecoming from Kailāsa to her mother Menakā at the autumn Durgā festival; with the vijayā songs of farewell, composed by Rāmprasād, Kamalākānta and others.
The devotee's affectionate reproach of the Mother for neglecting her child, a hallmark of the Śākta songs.
The Goddess coiled three and a half times around the Svayambhū liṅga at the base, led up through the centres to unite with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 51-53, Pūrṇānanda).
Kubjikā praised as 'coiled like a sleeping serpent' (Kubjikāmata 2.2).
The liṅga in the root centre around which Kuṇḍalinī lies coiled (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa).
The subtlest power in the crown centre within which is the abode of Śiva (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 49-50).
Worship of a young girl as the Goddess, prescribed in the eastern tantras (Rudrayāmala and others) and part of Durgā-pūjā in Bengal and of Kāmākhyā worship.
A vīra rite performed seated on a corpse in the cremation ground to win the Goddess's vision (as in the account of Sarvānanda). Restricted: named only.
A seat built over five skulls used for sādhana in Bengal (Tārāpīṭh; Ramakrishna's seat at Dakshineswar in the tradition's account). Restricted: named only.
The consort Śiva worshipped at each Mahāvidyā's right side (Toḍala 1.3-19).

The age in which only the path of the Āgama avails and Vedic mantras are powerless (Mahānirvāṇa 2.7-15); in which only householder and mendicant stages remain (8.8); in which, for the Kālīvilāsa, only the paśu disposition is allowed (4.2-3).
The haṃsa upon which the self rests, itself within the breath (Kubjikāmata 11.14).
One of the names of the final abode in the crown (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 50).
